notes.1a: Candidates were able to identify key definitions of a species, such as individuals breeding together to produce fertile offspring, but many candidates lost credit because they did not give any detail of the features, i.e. they did not state morphological, physiological, etc.
notes.1b: The most common problem here was giving allopatric speciation as an answer; ‘allopatric speciation’ is a term which implies geographical isolation, but does not explain how separation has been physically caused. �PAGE�59
notes.1c: Most candidates were awarded some credit here. It was obvious when candidates had learnt by rote the answer to this question, and perhaps had looked at past exam questions in order to identify key marking points for this style of question. Allopatric speciation was used in responses and described clearly. There were very few candidates who discussed the idea of the mating song not being recognised by the females, but good coverage of all other marking points. Mutations are not caused by environmental / selection pressures – they are random. Geographical isolation preventing gene flow was commonly confused with reproductive isolation should the two species meet.
notes.2a: (i) Some problems with describing the immune response were seen. T cells and B cells were frequently confused. Very few responses included the correct detail of how B cells bind the antigen; even fewer made reference to antigen-presenting cells. Credit was mostly awarded for references to plasma cells and antibodies.
notes.2aii: Candidates knew that a hybridoma cell is a plasma cell fused with a myeloma. ‘Mixing the cells’ was not enough; they needed to join together.
notes.2iii: Candidates struggled here; many seemed to understand the concept and knew that plasma cells cannot divide or grow in culture. They stated that myeloma cells will divide but did not specify indefinitely or continuously.
notes.2iv: Some candidates talked about markers, but did not qualify properly what the marker could have been attached to. Simply adding antigens to the solution would not identify hybridoma cells. Very few candidates suggested the use of labelled antigens or gave valid methods of marking or identifying the antigen. A small number gave other valid methods of identifying the hybridoma cells.
notes.2b: (i) This was a difficult question, not least because the graph required a lot of interpretation. Candidates would be well advised to make sure in descriptions of data that they clearly identify the trend. A common reason for not scoring marks here was incorrect reading of the results from the graph; group P is quite clearly 30.5% and not, for example, 30%. Many candidates stated that results in groups S and T were different; a 0.5% difference should not be considered meaningfully different. A proportion of the candidates simply wrote out the data in the graph but did not interpret in any way.
notes.2bii: Very few candidates were awarded credit for this question. Perhaps most candidates do not consider 71 people to be a small number, but in the context of this kind of investigation it is a small group.
notes.2c: A commonly given response was that monoclonal antibodies give a faster diagnosis, but many other points given referred to treatment, despite diagnosis being emphasised in the question.
notes.3a: Many candidates were unclear about this topic. They knew the movement of DNA to the anode, but failed to say that it was the phosphate group of the DNA that was negatively charged. Those who attempted to describe that lower mass moved faster were awarded, but candidates who wrote about the distance moved needed to include ‘per unit time’.
notes.3b: Candidates generally drew a band in the same place as the band for the HbA HbA individual, but did not correctly draw the second band above it.
notes.3c: Many candidates referred to checking family histories but did not give enough detail. A few mentioned genetic counselling. Many incorrect answers gave information concerning paternity testing and use in criminal investigations. �PAGE�60
notes.4a: Relatively few candidates answered this well. Some confused male and female parts of the flower, and pollen with seeds, while others did not use Fig. 4.1 and concentrate on the male parts of the flower. Even those who did focus on stamens frequently failed to relate their descriptions to increasing the likelihood of wind dislodging pollen. Most did not refer to anthers and those who did, only referred to half the answer, e.g. anthers outside of flower but no mention of pollen or long filament. Some thought that the anthers collected pollen. Many candidates referred to stigmas or stamens.
notes.4b: Most candidates scored well, identifying mutations, survival and reproduction for full credit. Candidates followed a well-rehearsed sequence of steps in describing an evolutionary change. However, some confused maize with corn borers, and the idea of resistant alleles was missed. Candidates used the term gene rather than alleles.
notes.4c: The homozygous recessive genotype rr was mostly given correctly.
notes.4d: The candidates appeared to have an understanding of the ideas, but their responses were not always detailed and concise enough score credit. Breeding non-resistant and resistant corn borers gave the heterozygote but they did not go on to say that these organisms would not be resistant or die.
notes.4e: (i) Many candidates were confused by the data and a fair number did not provide an answer at all. Mixing was identified but this was sometimes confused by also talking about mating. Some picked up on the variation in the results, and some noticed the discrepancy between males and females. Candidates tended to interpret the data in terms of missing (non-recaptured) borers having moved to other fields, rather than new (unmarked) borers having come from other fields.
notes.4eii: Candidates did not understand the impact of the strategy and what would be needed for it to be effective. Figures were quoted, but these did not relate to points being made and inbreeding occurring. The credit was mostly awarded for marked females mating with marked males or marked females mating with unmarked males.
notes.5a: Candidates knew the role of progesterone and answers were detailed. Common errors were to references to the uterus wall instead of the lining, and to implantation of the egg or ovum.
notes.5b: (i) Many candidates did not read to the smallest square of the graph and rounded their answer up to 33. Many missed the unit (days) and a few gave an incorrect unit, e.g. years.
notes.5bii: This was a difficult graph to interpret, but as with other questions, candidates should be encouraged to identify trends; many simply described each curve without using the data to answer the question. Many candidates stated that the different diets caused the rats to reach puberty, without giving any time span; they all reached puberty, so time was needed to make a comparison. As with any graph, there were a number of candidates who describe the y-axis variable affecting the x-axis variable, instead of the correct way around.
notes.6: This question was one of the best answered on the paper.
notes.6a: Candidates identified the reasons covering a range of marking points for species becoming endangered. They were also able to make links between pollination and a removal of flies.
notes.6b: (i) There was a lot of variation in the answers about the definition of the term biodiversity, but most candidates had learnt the definition and so gained credit here.
notes.6bii: Candidates had seen this type of question before and their answers showed the benefit of practising past papers. �PAGE�61
notes.7a: Many candidates wrote that the allele symbols were R and r, and then went on to carry out the cross perfectly, using the X and Y chromosome symbols in all genotypes in addition to the colour alleles. Common candidate errors included a number who did not include X and Y at all and scored no credit, or put superscripts on the Y chromosome. Most candidates were quite successful on this question.
notes.7b: (i) Candidates who were not awarded credit here pointed out that the son could only inherit the allele from the mother, but this was not really answering the question. Therefore, although they had scientific knowledge, they were not applying it tightly enough within the given context.
notes.7bii: Many candidates spoiled their answer of ‘heterozygous’ by adding dominant or recessive, however, many were awarded credit.
notes.7iii: There were many candidates whose answer ‘mutation’ did not score because more detail was required; they had not specified gene or allele mutation.
notes.8a: (i) Most candidates realised that the enzymes would denature. Some candidates were awarded some credit for discussing optimum temperature, (although some did not specify the enzyme), stomata, and reduction in Calvin cycle or increased photorespiration. It is important to note that less carbon dioxide (not no CO2) and a reduction in the Calvin Cycle (not cycle stops) are important points.
notes.8aii: Most candidates were credited for correctly drawing the likely curve. They were not as successful at explaining the curve. It was necessary to state that sorghum or C4 enzymes have a higher optimum temperature and give some structural feature which enabled the plant to avoid photorespiration. Some said it was adapted to an arid rather than a hot climate.
notes.8b: (i) Most candidates completed the table correctly.
notes.8bii: The graph was successfully completed by a majority of candidates. Those who did not score full credit made the usual mistakes. These included the axes being the wrong way around, the scales being incorrect, the units missing, points plotted incorrectly and a poorly drawn line.
notes.8iii: The definition of a limiting factor is always something candidates find difficult to explain. When a process is affected by more than one factor, the rate of the reaction is restricted by the factor that is nearest its lowest value. Section B
notes.9: Candidates answered this question very well and the majority chose this question rather than Question 10 on the kidney.
notes.9a: The question asked the candidates to describe how ATP is synthesised by oxidative phosphorylation. There was some confusion between NADH and NADPH and many missed out the hydrogen being released from the reduced NAD. Electrons accepted by ETC were mentioned, but no mention was made of carriers/cytochromes. Some candidates thought that it was hydrogen that moved rather than the hydrogen ion. Many candidates scored full credit here.
notes.9b: Another well answered question. The need for energy in living organisms was well known and examples were also given. Some missed the reference to light energy in photosynthesis and detail of the light dependent and light independent stages. All other energy requiring processes were well documented. �PAGE�62
notes.10a: Candidates were mostly well-prepared and in a few sentences or on a diagram were able to list at least six parts of the kidney. The only thing they were not used to doing was specifying which parts of the nephron were in the cortex and which in the medulla. Where diagrams were used they were used well, with correct labels and the position of nephron identified. Few candidates referred to the afferent and efferent arterioles or the capillary network.
notes.10b: Responses here were very varied from candidates who had shown a thorough knowledge of the functioning of the nephron. Many candidates gave a full account of ultrafiltration and then went on to reabsorption. There was confusion over where the sodium ions were moving from and to. Many gave a muddled account of the facilitated diffusion and cotransporters. Few mentioned osmosis. In the adaptations it was rare to see anything more than microvilli and many mitochondria. �PAGE�63
notes.key_messages:
• Accurate supporting figures, with the correct units, should be used when answering a question
accompanied by a table or graph.
• Candidates should be encouraged to look for an overall trend in figures or graphs and to be aware
that this is often more important than individual figures that may be showing minor fluctuations.
• In genetics, candidates should be given opportunities to carry out basic crosses so that they are
confident in the use of keys and use suitable symbols for genotypes.
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates had clearly used or referred to past papers when preparing for this exam. It is always
useful to practise past papers as some candidates have a good knowledge of biology but are unsure how to
express themselves clearly.
Command words such as ‘describe’, ‘explain’, ‘suggest’ and ‘compare’ require different responses from
candidates. If a description is required, including a reference to a graph or table, then it will be expected that
data will be used in the answer. Many candidates are able to do this effectively. An explanation requires
more than just a description and candidates should be encouraged to practise the difference between
‘explain’ and ‘describe’. A ‘suggest’ question encourages the candidate to display biological knowledge
linked to the learning outcome being tested. It is always worthwhile for a candidate to attempt an answer to
this sort of question as the mark scheme here will be fairly flexible
Finally, if a question requires a comparison then a candidate must refer to all of the variables being tested.
This was shown in Question 2(c) when it was not sufficient to simply state that diagnosis was fast. A better
approach is to refer to both in the same sentence or use ‘faster’ which shows a comparison. Words such as
‘whereas’ or ‘however’ can be used to link two parts of a sentence and therefore create a comparison.
Section B is an opportunity for candidates to display their knowledge of a learning outcome in a less
structured way. Much credit is available for answers in Section B and it is worth noting the credit allocations
for parts (a) and (b) whilst writing.
